screens.title: Account Address: what it is and how to present it
screens.narratorSegment: An Ethereum account address is the canonical identifier for a wallet, typically a 42-character hexadecimal string starting with 0x. Practically, that long string is not friendly to read or compare, so dApps format it. A common approach is truncation: keep the first six characters plus an ellipsis and the last four. This preserves distinguishability while staying compact. For example, 0x1234567890abcdef... fedc becomes 0x1234... fedc. Always offer a copy-to-clipboard affordance so users can get the full address for external tools. When displaying the address, include a clear label such as "Connected Wallet" and consider showing the network or chain ID to avoid cross-network mistakes. Don't assume address presence — guard against undefined currentAccount and show a friendly connect prompt or placeholder. A frequent misconception is that truncation hides the address entirely; it does not — you must still provide a straightforward copy option or a full-view modal when users need the complete value. Accessibility-wise, make sure the truncation and copy controls are reachable and announced properly. Closing question: how would you help a user confirm they're using the intended account when addresses look similar?

keyIdea.text: Truncate long hexadecimal addresses for readability, provide copy access, and label the wallet clearly to reduce mistakes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Account Address
Definition
An account address is a 42-character hex string that uniquely identifies a wallet on Ethereum. It is used as the source and destination for transactions.
Formatting patterns
  • Truncate display: keep first 6 and last 4 characters (e.g., 0x1234...abcd).
  • Provide a copy-to-clipboard affordance for the full address.
  • Label clearly as "Connected Wallet" and show chain if relevant.
Key Takeaway

Readable address format plus a copy option balances usability with precision.

Example
Connected Wallet: 0x123456...9abc
Scenario: The user has multiple wallets. Displaying a truncated address with a clear label and a copy action prevents the user from performing transactions from the wrong account. If addresses look similar, provide additional confirmation such as ENS names where available or a balance snapshot next to the address.
Common mistake
Showing the raw 42-char string without copy or truncation overwhelms the UI and increases user error.
Pro tip
Expose a full address view on click or via a copy button so power users can access the exact value when needed.

screens.title: Fetching ETH balance with web3.eth.getBalance
screens.narratorSegment: Fetching an account's native balance uses web3. eth. getBalance(account). This method returns the balance in Wei, and importantly it returns a string because blockchain values can exceed JavaScript's safe integer range. In a React component or provider, call getBalance inside a useEffect that depends on the web3 instance and the current account. Initialize the balance state to null so you can show a loading message rather than undefined. Wrap the fetch in a try-catch and set the balance to null or an error state on failure. When you receive the result, pass the Wei string to web3. utils. fromWei to convert to Ether before committing it to display state or format further. Remember to avoid performing arithmetic on the raw Wei string; either convert first or use a big-number library. A typical pattern in Web3Provider is to expose both the ethBalance state and a fetchEthBalance function, allowing components to trigger updates after transactions. Example walkthrough: inside useEffect, check web3 and accounts exist, then await web3. eth. getBalance(accounts[0]), convert with fromWei, and set state. End by asking: how will you show a loading state so the UI never attempts to render undefined values?

keyIdea.title: Fetch pattern
keyIdea.text: Call web3.eth.getBalance inside a useEffect, handle async errors, and convert Wei before display.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Fetch ETH balance
Code example (provider)
// inside Web3Provider
const [ethBalance, setEthBalance] = useState(null);

const fetchEthBalance = useCallback(async (account) => {
  if (web3 && account) {
    try {
      const balanceWei = await web3.eth.getBalance(account);
      const balanceEth = web3.utils.fromWei(balanceWei, 'ether');
      setEthBalance(balanceEth);
    } catch (error) {
      console.error('Error fetching ETH balance:', error);
      setEthBalance(null);
    }
  }
}, [web3]);

useEffect(() => {
  if (web3 && accounts.length) fetchEthBalance(accounts[0]);
}, [web3, accounts, fetchEthBalance]);
Explanation
  • getBalance returns a Wei string; do not treat it as a number directly.
  • Convert with web3.utils.fromWei before showing or formatting decimals.
  • Wrap calls in try-catch and handle loading with initial null state.
  • Expose fetchEthBalance so other components or actions can trigger updates.
Concrete example
If getBalance returns "1000000000000000000", converting with fromWei yields "1" which you then render as "1.0000 ETH" after formatting.
Key Takeaway

Always fetch in async effects, handle errors and loading, and convert Wei to Ether before display.

screens.title: Converting Wei to Ether safely
screens.narratorSegment: Wei is the smallest unit of Ether: one Ether equals 10 to the 18th Wei. Because getBalance returns a Wei string, conversion is required before display. Web3. js provides web3. utils. fromWei(weiString, 'ether') which returns a decimal string representing Ether. After conversion, format the string to a reasonable number of decimals for UI readability, for example four decimal places. Avoid converting Wei using native JavaScript division because precision will be lost; always use the provided utility or a big-number library when doing arithmetic. In a component, after converting, store the formatted string in state and render it with the ETH label: for example, display "1.2345 ETH". Also consider edge cases: very small balances like 0.0000000000001 ETH may render as 0.0000 after rounding; decide whether to show more precision or a label like "< 0.0001 ETH". A common misconception is that conversion yields a numeric type ready for math; the result is a string and should be parsed into a big-number type if you need arithmetic. In summary, convert with fromWei, then format for readability, and only use numeric math via a big-number library when necessary.

keyIdea.title: Conversion rule
keyIdea.text: Use web3.utils.fromWei to convert Wei strings to Ether, then format decimals for clear display; avoid native division for precision.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Wei → Ether
Conversion example
const balanceWei = await web3.eth.getBalance(account);
const balanceEthString = web3.utils.fromWei(balanceWei, 'ether');
// Format to 4 decimals for display
const display = parseFloat(balanceEthString).toFixed(4) + ' ETH';
Note: fromWei returns a string. Use parseFloat or a safe numeric formatter for display, but use big-number libraries for precise arithmetic.
Guidance and edge cases
  • Very small Ether values may round to zero; consider a "< 0.0001 ETH" display.
  • Do not perform arithmetic on raw Wei strings with Number; convert to BigNumber first or use fromWei.
  • Keep the ETH label visible to prevent confusion with token balances or fiat values.
Concrete example
If getBalance returns "1000000000000000", fromWei yields "0.001" and showing "0.0010 ETH" communicates a clear, rounded value.
Key Takeaway

Always convert Wei using web3.utils.fromWei, then format for readability; avoid native number math on Wei strings.

screens.title: Implementing polling to update balances
screens.narratorSegment: Polling is a simple technique to keep a displayed native balance in sync with the blockchain. The pattern is: fetch the balance immediately when the account or web3 instance becomes available, then set up a setInterval to re-fetch at a reasonable cadence, such as every ten seconds. Important details: store the interval identifier so you can clear it in the cleanup function returned by useEffect; otherwise your app will leak timers when the component unmounts or the account changes. Also avoid overlapping requests — ensure the previous fetch is complete or throttle calls. If you expose fetchEthBalance from the provider, call it inside the interval rather than duplicating logic. When polling, consider the trade-offs: more frequent polling reduces delay but increases node/network usage. If you're using a rate-limited node provider, lengthen the interval. As an optimization, re-fetch immediately after transactions you initiate are confirmed to provide a near-instant update without continuous high-frequency polling. A misconception to avoid is trusting the UI to be immediately up-to-date when you only poll occasionally; communicate the last update time if exact freshness is needed. How often will you poll given your node provider limits?

keyIdea.title: Polling pattern
keyIdea.text: Fetch on mount, poll at a reasonable interval, prevent overlapping calls, and clear intervals in cleanup to avoid leaks.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Polling for updates
Safe polling pattern
useEffect(() => {
  let intervalId;
  if (web3 && accounts.length) {
    fetchEthBalance(accounts[0]);
    intervalId = setInterval(() => fetchEthBalance(accounts[0]), 10000);
  }
  return () => clearInterval(intervalId);
}, [web3, accounts, fetchEthBalance]);
Key: clearInterval in cleanup and avoid creating multiple overlapping intervals when inputs change.
Trade-offs and tips
  • Short intervals give fresher data but increase network load and node costs.
  • If using a paid provider, choose an interval that balances responsiveness and request quotas.
  • Throttle or debounce to avoid overlapping requests if a fetch is still running.
Concrete example
Poll every 10 seconds for a general UI and re-fetch immediately after a confirmed transaction that affects the account balance.

screens.title: Re-fetching after transactions for efficiency
screens.narratorSegment: A more efficient approach than continuous high-frequency polling is to re-fetch the balance after transactions your dApp initiates are confirmed. When you send a transaction, the transaction receipt or confirmation event indicates that on-chain state has changed. At confirmation, call fetchEthBalance for the affected account. This gives near-immediate feedback to the user who initiated the action without aggressive polling. Implementation detail: your transaction flow should await confirmation via the web3 provider's send or subscribe APIs and then call the provider's balance fetch function. Combine this with a lighter polling interval as a fallback for external transactions the dApp didn't initiate. Also expose fetchEthBalance publicly from the Web3Provider so UI components or transaction handlers can call it after confirmations. A common pitfall is assuming a transaction is final immediately; use confirmed receipts and avoid updating on unmined transactions. This hybrid approach—confirm-triggered fetch plus low-rate polling—keeps network requests reasonable while providing timely updates for user-driven changes. Re-fetching after transactions for efficiency means re-fetch after confirmed transactions to give timely feedback while keeping polling rates low for other changes.. In practical terms, update the balance right after your dapp's transactions confirm to reduce polling needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Post-transaction update
Implementation sketch
// after sending a tx
const receipt = await web3.eth.sendTransaction(txParams);
if (receipt && receipt.status) {
  // Transaction confirmed — re-fetch balance
  fetchEthBalance(currentAccount);
}
Use the transaction receipt status or a confirmation event to determine when to re-fetch. This gives instant feedback for your user's action.
Why this helps
  • Reduces unnecessary node requests compared to aggressive polling.
  • Provides immediate, relevant feedback after user actions initiated in your dApp.
  • Combine with light polling to catch external transfers.
Common Mistake

Updating the UI on an unconfirmed transaction can mislead users. Wait for confirmed receipts for balance updates.

screens.title: Loading state and error handling
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable UI must handle loading and error states when fetching balances. Initialize your balance state to null, not undefined, so components can distinguish between 'not fetched yet' and 'zero balance'. While the fetch is in progress, show a short message such as "Fetching balance..." or a subtle spinner; avoid rendering numeric placeholders that later change to the real number, which causes layout shift. On error, display a clear but non-alarming message such as "Unable to fetch balance" and offer a retry action or a hint to check network connection. When using polling, prevent rapid UI updates that flash intermediate values; update the display only when the new value differs meaningfully or after a debounce. A common misconception is to set balance to 0 on error—this hides the fact that the value couldn't be retrieved. Instead, preserve null or an explicit error state. In your provider, consider exposing isLoading and error alongside ethBalance so components can render appropriate UI. Final question: how will you communicate stale data versus a real zero balance? Loading state and error handling means use null for initial state, show a loading indicator, and surface errors rather than defaulting to zero to avoid misleading users.. In practical terms, avoid ui flicker and show clear messages while balance data is pending or failed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Loading & Error Handling
Comparison: good vs bad
Bad
Set balance to 0 on error and don't show loading—users are misled into thinking they have zero funds.
Good
Use null initially, show "Fetching balance...", and show an explicit error state with retry options.

function useAccountBalance(web3, account) {

  const fetch = useCallback(async () => { ... }, [web3, account]);

screens.title: Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Working with wallet addresses and balances has a few recurring pitfalls. First, treating getBalance's returned value as a number leads to precision and overflow problems; remember it's a string representing Wei. Convert with fromWei or use big-number utilities for arithmetic. Second, failing to handle loading state produces UI flicker or runtime errors when attempting to format undefined; initialize balance to null and show a loading message. Third, aggressive polling without cleanup can cause memory leaks or exceed node request quotas; always clear intervals in useEffect cleanups and choose a sensible interval. Fourth, updating the display immediately on unconfirmed transactions can mislead users; wait for confirmed receipts before assuming final balances. Finally, poor address display without a copy option or label increases user error. For each pitfall, implement the recommended fix: use fromWei, null-state + loader, cleanup timers, confirm-before-update, and truncate + copy UI. Closing question: which pitfall caused the most trouble in your own dApp builds? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on two practical tasks you will implement right away: showing the connected Ethereum account and showing that account's native balance in a friendly format. You will learn how to read the currentAccount supplied by your Web3 provider, why Ethereum addresses are shown truncated for readability, and how to fetch the raw Wei balance with Web3. js then convert that value to Ether for display. We'll also cover strategies to keep that balance accurate over time, including safe polling and re-checking after transactions confirm. These steps are essential because users trust a dApp that clearly identifies their wallet and shows up-to-date funds. A common usability mistake is displaying raw blockchain values or leaving the UI in a loading state; you'll learn how to avoid both. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to present a formatted address, fetch and format a balance using web3. utils. fromWei, and integrate periodic or event-driven updates so the UI reflects the true on-chain state. Think about why a clean address display and accurate balance increase user trust—that is the goal here.

These four learning objectives focus your work on practical skills you will apply immediately. First, you will retrieve and render the connected Ethereum account address from your Web3 provider so users always know which wallet is active. Second, you will fetch the native currency balance using web3. eth. getBalance and present it after converting from Wei to Ether for human readability. Third, you will implement a strategy to keep that balance current: simple polling with cleanup or re-fetching after transactions confirm. Fourth, you'll learn how to format and present blockchain values inside React components, including handling loading states and string-typed balances. Each objective pairs a coding skill with a usability rationale: formatted addresses reduce cognitive load, converted balances let users make financial decisions, timely updates keep the dApp trustworthy, and careful state handling avoids UI flicker and runtime errors. Practice these steps in the provider and in a display component so logic and UI remain separated. As you work, notice one common misconception: treating balances as numbers before conversion leads to precision errors. Keep balances as strings until converted by web3. utils. fromWei or handled by a proper big-number utility.

This second objectives screen drills into how you turn the four goals into concrete practice. For retrieving an address, ensure your Web3Provider exposes currentAccount through a hook and render a truncated string in your header. For fetching balances, call web3. eth. getBalance and remember it returns a Wei string; convert that string with web3. utils. fromWei to produce Ether for display. For updates, choose a strategy: simple polling at an interval and clear it in the effect cleanup, or trigger a fetch after transactions initiated by your application are confirmed. For formatting, round to a fixed number of decimals, append the currency label, and show a loading state while fetching. Each card here pairs the technical step with a small mnemonic or visual cue so you can remember the trade-offs. A common error is making arithmetic on Wei strings instead of using big-number libraries or converting to Ether first. Keep the provider thin and expose a fetch function so multiple components can reuse the same balance logic.

An Ethereum account address is the canonical identifier for a wallet, typically a 42-character hexadecimal string starting with 0x. Practically, that long string is not friendly to read or compare, so dApps format it. A common approach is truncation: keep the first six characters plus an ellipsis and the last four. This preserves distinguishability while staying compact. For example, 0x1234567890abcdef... fedc becomes 0x1234... fedc. Always offer a copy-to-clipboard affordance so users can get the full address for external tools. When displaying the address, include a clear label such as "Connected Wallet" and consider showing the network or chain ID to avoid cross-network mistakes. Don't assume address presence — guard against undefined currentAccount and show a friendly connect prompt or placeholder. A frequent misconception is that truncation hides the address entirely; it does not — you must still provide a straightforward copy option or a full-view modal when users need the complete value. Accessibility-wise, make sure the truncation and copy controls are reachable and announced properly. Closing question: how would you help a user confirm they're using the intended account when addresses look similar?

Fetching an account's native balance uses web3. eth. getBalance(account). This method returns the balance in Wei, and importantly it returns a string because blockchain values can exceed JavaScript's safe integer range. In a React component or provider, call getBalance inside a useEffect that depends on the web3 instance and the current account. Initialize the balance state to null so you can show a loading message rather than undefined. Wrap the fetch in a try-catch and set the balance to null or an error state on failure. When you receive the result, pass the Wei string to web3. utils. fromWei to convert to Ether before committing it to display state or format further. Remember to avoid performing arithmetic on the raw Wei string; either convert first or use a big-number library. A typical pattern in Web3Provider is to expose both the ethBalance state and a fetchEthBalance function, allowing components to trigger updates after transactions. Example walkthrough: inside useEffect, check web3 and accounts exist, then await web3. eth. getBalance(accounts[0]), convert with fromWei, and set state. End by asking: how will you show a loading state so the UI never attempts to render undefined values?

Wei is the smallest unit of Ether: one Ether equals 10 to the 18th Wei. Because getBalance returns a Wei string, conversion is required before display. Web3. js provides web3. utils. fromWei(weiString, 'ether') which returns a decimal string representing Ether. After conversion, format the string to a reasonable number of decimals for UI readability, for example four decimal places. Avoid converting Wei using native JavaScript division because precision will be lost; always use the provided utility or a big-number library when doing arithmetic. In a component, after converting, store the formatted string in state and render it with the ETH label: for example, display "1.2345 ETH". Also consider edge cases: very small balances like 0.0000000000001 ETH may render as 0.0000 after rounding; decide whether to show more precision or a label like "< 0.0001 ETH". A common misconception is that conversion yields a numeric type ready for math; the result is a string and should be parsed into a big-number type if you need arithmetic. In summary, convert with fromWei, then format for readability, and only use numeric math via a big-number library when necessary.

Polling is a simple technique to keep a displayed native balance in sync with the blockchain. The pattern is: fetch the balance immediately when the account or web3 instance becomes available, then set up a setInterval to re-fetch at a reasonable cadence, such as every ten seconds. Important details: store the interval identifier so you can clear it in the cleanup function returned by useEffect; otherwise your app will leak timers when the component unmounts or the account changes. Also avoid overlapping requests — ensure the previous fetch is complete or throttle calls. If you expose fetchEthBalance from the provider, call it inside the interval rather than duplicating logic. When polling, consider the trade-offs: more frequent polling reduces delay but increases node/network usage. If you're using a rate-limited node provider, lengthen the interval. As an optimization, re-fetch immediately after transactions you initiate are confirmed to provide a near-instant update without continuous high-frequency polling. A misconception to avoid is trusting the UI to be immediately up-to-date when you only poll occasionally; communicate the last update time if exact freshness is needed. How often will you poll given your node provider limits?

A more efficient approach than continuous high-frequency polling is to re-fetch the balance after transactions your dApp initiates are confirmed. When you send a transaction, the transaction receipt or confirmation event indicates that on-chain state has changed. At confirmation, call fetchEthBalance for the affected account. This gives near-immediate feedback to the user who initiated the action without aggressive polling. Implementation detail: your transaction flow should await confirmation via the web3 provider's send or subscribe APIs and then call the provider's balance fetch function. Combine this with a lighter polling interval as a fallback for external transactions the dApp didn't initiate. Also expose fetchEthBalance publicly from the Web3Provider so UI components or transaction handlers can call it after confirmations. A common pitfall is assuming a transaction is final immediately; use confirmed receipts and avoid updating on unmined transactions. This hybrid approach—confirm-triggered fetch plus low-rate polling—keeps network requests reasonable while providing timely updates for user-driven changes. Re-fetching after transactions for efficiency means re-fetch after confirmed transactions to give timely feedback while keeping polling rates low for other changes.. In practical terms, update the balance right after your dapp's transactions confirm to reduce polling needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A reliable UI must handle loading and error states when fetching balances. Initialize your balance state to null, not undefined, so components can distinguish between 'not fetched yet' and 'zero balance'. While the fetch is in progress, show a short message such as "Fetching balance..." or a subtle spinner; avoid rendering numeric placeholders that later change to the real number, which causes layout shift. On error, display a clear but non-alarming message such as "Unable to fetch balance" and offer a retry action or a hint to check network connection. When using polling, prevent rapid UI updates that flash intermediate values; update the display only when the new value differs meaningfully or after a debounce.
